All other diagnoses in the differential either lack the degree of GGT elevation (e.g., Alagille may have normal/mildly elevated GGT; PFIC types 1 & 2 are typically GGT-low), present with extrahepatic features (e.g., cardiac/ocular in Alagille), or would be expected to show clearer metabolic/infectious markers — none of which are yet reported.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Infant aged 4 weeks — peak age for presentation of biliary atresia  
- Progressive jaundice for 2 weeks — consistent with insidious onset of biliary obstruction  
- Pale (acholic) stools — hallmark of impaired bile flow into duodenum  
- Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: direct bilirubin 12.3 mg/dL (82% of total) — confirms cholestasis  
- Markedly elevated ALP (2007 U/L) — reflects cholangiocyte/bone activity; high in cholestasis  
- Elevated GGT (154 U/L) — strongly supports obstructive or severe hepatocellular cholestasis; argues against low-GGT causes (e.g., PFIC1/2, galactosemia)  
- Mild transaminitis (AST 53, ALT 45) — indicates concomitant hepatocellular injury, common in early biliary atresia  
- Formerly breastfed, now on formula — rules out prolonged breastfeeding jaundice (which is unconjugated)  

[GAPS]  
- Abdominal ultrasound findings (e.g., triangular cord sign, absent gallbladder, hepatic artery Doppler) — critical to assess for biliary atresia  
- HIDA scan result — functional assessment of biliary excretion; failure to visualize bowel is highly suggestive of biliary atresia  
- Liver biopsy histopathology — may show ductular proliferation, portal fibrosis, bile plugs — supportive but not definitive alone  
- Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level — typically markedly elevated in biliary atresia vs. lower in many metabolic/infectious causes  
- PT/INR — to assess synthetic dysfunction; coagulopathy may develop later in biliary atresia but is not early-sensitive  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Biliary atresia
